### Technical Summary
In BERT, Masked Language Modeling (MLM) is an unsupervised pre-training objective where some percentage of input tokens are masked at random and the model is trained to predict the original vocabulary tokens using deep bidirectional context [1].

### Technical Breakdown & Mechanism
- **Bidirectional Representation**: Standard conditional language models can only be trained left-to-right or right-to-left, because bidirectional conditioning would allow tokens to indirectly see themselves. MLM solves this by masking input tokens at random and conditioning jointly on both left and right context [1].
- **Masking Strategy**: In all experiments, BERT masks 15% of all WordPiece tokens in each sequence at random [1].
- **Mitigating Pre-training/Fine-tuning Mismatch**: To prevent mismatch since the `[MASK]` token never appears during fine-tuning, the data generator replaces the chosen 15% of tokens with:
  1. The `[MASK]` token 80% of the time [1].
  2. A random token 10% of the time [1].
  3. The unchanged original token 10% of the time [1].
- **Prediction Objective**: The final hidden vectors corresponding to the masked tokens are fed into an output softmax over the vocabulary, trained with cross-entropy loss [1].

Unlike standard conditional language models that are unidirectional, MLM allows the representation to fuse left and right context, enabling deep bidirectional pre-training.

### Technical Summary
BERT supports both fine-tuning and feature-based approaches for downstream natural language processing tasks [1], [2].

### Comparison: Fine-Tuning vs. Feature-Based Approaches
1. **Fine-Tuning Approach**: In the fine-tuning approach, the pre-trained BERT model parameters are used as initialization, and all parameters are updated end-to-end downstream with minimal task-specific modifications [1]. This provides a unified architecture across diverse sentence-level and token-level tasks [1].
2. **Feature-Based Approach**: In the feature-based approach (evaluated in Section 5.3 on CoNLL-2003 NER), fixed feature representations are extracted from pre-trained BERT layers (e.g. concatenating the last 4 hidden layers) and fed into a task-specific model without updating the underlying BERT weights [2].
3. **Practical Trade-offs**: Feature-based approaches offer computational efficiency advantages by pre-computing representations once, while fine-tuning provides superior accuracy and end-to-end simplicity across most tasks [1], [2].
